security_spec.violation_condition: The XiangShan IOPMP RTL (IopmpChecker.scala) references ERR_CFG.msi_en as both the MSI/wired-interrupt selection control at ERR_CFG bit 3 AND as the implicit gate for ERR_MSIADDRH availability (line 497 comment: 'if ERR_CFG.msi_en = 1'). After this PR, the spec renames ERR_CFG bit 3 to msi_sel (same bit, different semantic role) and adds a new read-only HWCFG2.msi_en at HWCFG2 bit 26 as the authoritative MSI-extension-presence indicator. The RTL neither implements HWCFG2.msi_en at bit 26 (the RegHwcfg2 bundle has no msi_en field; the reserved gap at bits 25:18 already splits differently from the new spec's rsv at 25:18 + msi_en at 26) nor updates the ERR_MSIADDRH availability gating to check HWCFG2.msi_en instead of ERR_CFG.msi_en. Software reading HWCFG2 bit 26 gets a reserved-field value (likely 0), concludes MSI is unsupported, and skips MSI configuration even though the RTL actually implements the MSI write path (RegErrmsiaddr, RegErrmsiaddrh, msidata, msi_werr are all instantiated).
security_spec.summary: Missing HWCFG2.msi_en RO bit and stale ERR_CFG.msi_en naming in RTL cause MSI extension presence detection to fail: software trusts HWCFG2.msi_en==0 and disables MSI, but RTL unconditionally implements MSI registers and the MSI write-trigger path, creating a silent MSI capability deadlock where neither wired nor MSI interrupt works correctly
